transcript:
00:00 - Carlos Mendez: Hey everyone, this is Carlos from Redwood, thanks for joining. We got about 50 minutes, we'll do a quick SDK hands-on, auth, then the Console and Optimize hints. Priya's gonna jump into the code.
00:22 - Maya Patel: Hey Carlos, thanks, excited. Just so you know, Laura might need to hop off around 16:00 for another meeting.
01:10 - Priya Desai: Cool, thanks Maya. Quick check: are you planning to run on Redwood hosted at first or try Dedicated?
01:35 - Samir Khan: Probably hosted to start, we want to get something live for holiday traffic, but if costs spike we may move to dedicated. Main ask is predictable p95 latency under 400ms for short prompts.
02:00 - Evan Liu: Got it. We'll show both patterns — hosted quickstart and notes for Dedicated and Private. For the quickstart we'll use the Python SDK then show TypeScript bits.
05:15 - Priya Desai: Ok opening the quickstart repo link I posted in the chat (link: https://app.redwood.dev/sandbox/vela-quickstart). First step pip install redwood-sdk, or npm i @redwood/inference. In Python example the auth can be via REDWOOD_API_KEY in your environment or via the SSO token exchange for enterprise customers.
12:30 - Jordan Peters: Quick question — how do you recommend storing keys in CI? We use GitHub Actions.
12:48 - Priya Desai: Great question. We recommend GitHub Secrets or your org KMS. Set the key as REDWOOD_API_KEY in the secret store, then reference it in actions: env: REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }}. For private deployments you'd swap to a short-lived role token via OIDC.
15:00 - Laura Chen: For SSO we need SAML — do you have a sample flow?
15:18 - Carlos Mendez: Yes, we have a SAML quickstart for Console login and role mapping. I'll send the SAML metadata + mapping doc. Note though: API access via SSO usually maps to service accounts — we can show that after the quickstart.
20:00 - Priya Desai: Now in the Python quickstart, here's a common pitfall — devs put the API key in repo root .env and accidentally commit. We recommend a template .env.example and .gitignore. Also show snippet: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
20:35 - Priya Desai: For TypeScript: import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
25:00 - Samir Khan: When you say Optimize, are you talking about the Console recommendations or an automated agent?
25:20 - Priya Desai: Console Optimize provides prescriptive suggestions — batching window, cache TTLs, quantization profiles based on the model and sequence distribution. It also surfaces estimated token cost impact. The runtime has continuous batching and KV/prefix caching.
30:15 - Priya Desai: If you expect many short prompts (like product search), we suggest prefix cache and small batch sizes with a 30ms gather window. For long-form generation, switch to larger batch sizes and different model variants.
33:00 - Maya Patel: Any gotchas for embeddings and when we run semantic search?
33:20 - Evan Liu: Use dedicated or pin a model variant with higher throughput for embeddings, because embeddings are often CPU/GPU heavy; we also suggest batching and async pipelines in the client. Embedding cost can be minimized with quantized models on Dedicated.
36:40 - Priya Desai: Back to auth — KMS integration: we support customer KMS for Private deployments and we can integrate with AWS KMS or your HSM for key wrapping. For hosted API we recommend token rotation via our API and storing wrapped keys in Secrets Manager.
40:30 - Jordan Peters: How does VPC/private deployment affect latency for global users?
40:50 - Evan Liu: VPC/private keeps control-plane and telemetry inside your network, but region routing still matters. For global, you can use multi-region Dedicated pools or fallback routing to hosted to avoid outages. There's a tradeoff — private sometimes adds a little extra network hop.
44:10 - Priya Desai: Quick demo: I'm sending a generation request from the Python quickstart. (typing) You might see streaming chunks in the Console live trace. Note the trace ID, you can paste it into the Console for per-token latencies.
46:00 - Maya Patel: I see the trace, the p50 is low but p95 spikes when QPS hits about 120 — is that expected?
46:22 - Priya Desai: Yes, you likely need a dedicated pool or autoscale bump. For sudden spikes we recommend burst capacity or an autoscaling policy in Dedicated with a warm pool.
48:00 - Carlos Mendez: Quick recap before we run the pilot checklist: we'll give you sandbox creds, Priya will push quickstart repos, Jordan will provide traffic profile, and we'll schedule a perf baseline.
50:10 - Laura Chen: Sounds good, can you also include security artefacts — SOC2, ISO, and a sample audit log export?
50:28 - Carlos Mendez: Absolutely, I'll attach the security pack in the follow-up.
51:30 - Maya Patel: Thanks all, that was helpful. We'll review the quickstart and aim to get the perf numbers to you next week.
51:50 - Carlos Mendez: Perfect, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and the next call invite.
